source.title: A Convergence Analysis of Gradient Descent for Deep Linear Neural Networks
source.authors: Sanjeev Arora; N. Cohen; Noah Golowich; Wei Hu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes gradient descent and reports its own convergence experiments, but on deep linear regression networks and a nonlinear MNIST network rather than the CIFAR classification settings named in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports convergence results for its own deep linear and MNIST experiments, plus explicit theoretical convergence and failure claims. Figure 1 values are not numerically transcribed in the supplied text; no exact values are inferred from the plots. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4's initialization-dependent training speed and depth through convergence experiments and theory for plain linear networks, plus a ReLU MNIST experiment. It does not test batch normalization or the other versions' specified behaviors.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. Add the sufficiently small learning-rate requirement and clarify that the initialization assumptions are necessary for the general guarantee because counterexamples exist when either is dropped; they are not proven necessary for every successful run. The empirical conclusion is favorable convergence in the tested linear regression and ReLU MNIST settings.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical gradient-descent analysis and experiments on deep linear regression, plus an exploratory nonlinear MNIST experiment; the versions concern different models, datasets and interventions. No CIFAR classification experiment or batch-normalization comparison is reported.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization standard deviation and network depth changed convergence in the layer-wise independent linear-regression experiments; balanced initialization improved convergence across the tested standard deviations. The paper also gives theoretical failure cases when either approximate balancedness or deficiency margin is absent.

fits_no_version.finding: Approximate weight balancedness persists during the independently initialized depth-three regression run.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient descent approximately preserves differences between adjacent layers' Gram matrices when initialization is sufficiently balanced.

record.problems: The main experiments are small and use a single scalar regression dataset; plotted results are described qualitatively without per-setting numerical values in the supplied text. The MNIST experiment reports loss after 10 epochs and does not test CIFAR classification. The theoretical guarantees rely on restrictive assumptions, including whitened data, squared loss, linear networks, approximate balancedness and positive deficiency margin.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were extracted from Figure 1 for each initialization standard deviation because the supplied text does not give the individual plotted values. The paper's cited findings from other studies and initialization-probability calculations that do not report gradient-descent outcomes were excluded.

untested.parts: Training classification error in large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and the stated model-size and regularization comparisons.
Spurious local minima and extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth degradation in batch-normalized convolutional networks and its prevention by residual shortcuts, tanh initialization, or Fixup.

Activation-specific initialization comparisons, direct signal and gradient propagation measurements, orthogonal versus variance-matched Gaussian tanh networks, and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Recovery above the initial stability threshold and curvature or sharpness dynamics.
Batch normalization's effects on accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance, and normalization-free residual training with Fixup.

missing.what: The positive convergence guarantees: Theorem 1 gives linear convergence at arbitrary depth under approximate balancedness, positive deficiency margin, sufficient rank capacity, and an explicit learning-rate bound; Theorem 2 establishes a constant-probability guarantee for balanced Gaussian end-to-end initialization in scalar regression.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source listed for V4. Exact plotted values cannot be recovered from the supplied text; the qualitative convergence comparisons are explicitly stated. Balanced initialization is a different intervention from activation-specific variance matching, so these results support the broader initialization dependence without establishing V4's specific tanh and convolutional examples.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 classification error, convolutional networks, random or corrupted labels, and comparisons with smaller models or regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and the effect of extra student neurons.
Plain versus residual nonlinear convolutional networks as a function of depth.
Activation-matched initializations, deep tanh networks, orthogonal weights and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning rates above a stability threshold, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and full-batch stability behavior.
Batch-normalization comparisons, learning-rate tolerance and the Fixup recipe.

rows.subject: three layer network (N = 3) with hidden widths (d1, d2) set to 32
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on whitened scalar regression with layer-wise independent zero-centered Gaussian initialization; initialization standard deviation varied and learning rate grid-searched for each standard deviation.

conditions.value: UCI Machine Learning Repository “Ethanol” problem; 2565 examples, 128 features
layer-wise independent Gaussian perturbations centered at zero
grid-searched independently for each standard deviation

rows.measure: Iterations to reach training loss within 10^-5 from optimal training loss.
rows.value: A range of standard deviations led to fast convergence (a few hundred iterations or less); below and above it optimization decelerated by orders of magnitude (Figure 1(a), values not stated).
rows.note: The paper describes a narrow effective initialization range and slow convergence outside it; exact per-standard-deviation measurements are figure-only.
rows.check: The initialization effect is clear, not partial: an intermediate scale converges in hundreds of iterations or fewer, while smaller and larger scales slow training by orders of magnitude. Identify the network as linear.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, three-layer ethanol regression experiment; Figure 1(a).

rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on the same whitened scalar regression task with layer-wise independent zero-centered Gaussian initialization; initialization standard deviation varied and learning rate grid-searched.

conditions.value: layer-wise independent Gaussian perturbations centered at zero
grid-searched independently for each standard deviation

rows.measure: Iterations to reach training loss within 10^-5 from optimal training loss.
rows.baseline: three layer model under same protocol (reported comparison)
rows.value: The effective standard-deviation band was narrower than for the three-layer model; outside it convergence was extremely slow and did not take place within 10^6 iterations.
rows.note: The paper reports the depth comparison explicitly but does not provide exact per-setting iteration counts in the text.
rows.check: The narrower successful initialization range at eight layers directly shows initialization-dependent trainable depth. Failure outside that range supports this dependence rather than making the effect partial. Identify the network as linear.

rows.measure: Iterations to reach training loss within 10^-5 from optimal training loss.

rows.subject: depth-3 network, run with standard deviation s = 10^-3
rows.operation_detail: Measured weight balancedness during the layer-wise independently initialized gradient-descent run.
rows.baseline: initial degree at initialization, not stated numerically
rows.value: Approximate balancedness persists under gradient descent (Figure 1(c); values not stated).
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative description; the figure provides no transcribed numerical values.
rows.check: Persistence of weight balancedness is a mechanism measurement; it does not itself measure training speed, trainable depth, or signal and gradient propagation.

rows.subject: fully-connected non-linear neural network of the MNIST tutorial built into TensorFlow
rows.operation_detail: SGD training with ReLU and softmax-cross-entropy; initialization standard deviation varied, then repeated using balanced initialization based on Gaussian perturbations centered at zero.

conditions.value: customary layer-wise independent Gaussian versus balanced initialization; both Gaussian perturbations centered at zero

rows.value: Balanced initialization led to improved (faster and more stable) convergence across the tested initialization standard deviations (Figure 1(d); numerical values not stated).
rows.note: Authors explicitly state that the theoretical analysis does not cover nonlinear activation, softmax-cross-entropy or stochastic optimization. This comparison tests initialization effects, not batch normalization.
rows.check: Remove V6: there is no normalization comparison. The authors explicitly report faster, more stable convergence, so partial is unwarranted. The measured outcome is loss after 10 epochs, not time to a fixed loss.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, final experiment; Figure 1(d); Appendix E, nonlinear initialization implementation.

rows.subject: deep linear neural network with even depth and uniform input, output and hidden dimension d
rows.size_stated: even depth N; all dimensions equal to d
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical counterexample: choose unbalanced initial weights whose end-to-end matrix has deficiency margin, then apply gradient descent at any learning rate.
rows.measure: Whether the objective can converge below a positive constant.
rows.value: For some initializations, convergence fails and the objective never goes beneath a positive constant, for any learning rate.
rows.note: A theoretical counterexample shows initialization can prevent convergence; it does not test activation-matched initialization.
rows.check: Failure under severely unbalanced initialization is consistent with V4's initialization dependence, not reversed. Correct the quantifiers: for each chosen learning rate, a failing initialization is constructed; one fixed initialization is not shown to fail for every learning rate.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C, Claim 4; Appendix D.6, learning-rate-dependent initialization construction.

rows.subject: deep linear neural network with even depth and uniform input, output and hidden dimension d
rows.size_stated: even depth N; all dimensions equal to d
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical counterexample: identity initialization is perfectly balanced, but the target is symmetric with at least one negative eigenvalue, so deficiency margin is absent.

conditions.value: symmetric Φ with at least one negative eigenvalue

rows.measure: Whether training loss can converge to zero.
rows.value: Gradient descent fails: the objective never goes beneath a positive constant.
rows.note: This is a theoretical failure case showing balancedness alone is insufficient.
rows.check: Identity initialization preserves signals initially but does not yield convergence in this construction. This is failure of the proposed benefit, not an opposite-direction speed effect. The result concerns even-depth linear networks and symmetric targets with a negative eigenvalue.
